toc.text: 10. Adoption Dashboards and the BusinessAnalyst Permission Set
12. Change Management Across the Delivery Life Cycle

html:
The most technically perfect Salesforce implementation delivers zero value if the people who must use it do not change their behavior. Change management plans the people side of the rollout: who is affected, what changes for them, why now, and how they are brought along. This phase covers adoption readiness, persona-based training plans, business-language release notes, communication cadence, and the platform metrics that prove whether behavior actually changed.

By the end you will be able to take the signed deliverables of Phase 12 — the known-issues list, the sign-off date, the modules users have already touched — and turn them into a change plan that keeps BrightLogistics dispatchers, managers, and admins actually using the new CRM.

Learning Objectives

  • Assess adoption readiness on an account, ...
  • Write a training plan matched to learner personas, ...
  • Prepare concise release notes and communications, ...
  • Measure adoption with platform metrics, ...
  • Iterate support after go-live, ...
  • Plan the comms channel and cadence for each stakeholder group, ...
  • Build an adoption dashboard from baseline and target KPIs, ...
  • Diagnose declining usage by persona before changing anything, ...

1. Adoption Is a Design Goal

Delivery teams measure "done" as deploy date; the business measures it as working differently. The cleanest fit-gap and the cleanest sign-off mean nothing if dispatchers keep passing leads by email. Adoption must be designed in from the start, not repaired after launch.

Change management answers one question: who is affected, what changes for them, how do we bring them along? BrightLogistics groups are clear — reps to the new lead flow, managers to dashboard KPIs, admins to new objects and automation. Each changes differently; each needs a different support plan.

PersonaChangeSupport
Sales repsNew lead flow, auto-assignment2h demo + cheat sheet, office hours
ManagersDashboard KPIs replace Excel reportsReport walkthrough, weekly pulse
AdminsNew objects, flows, approval processConfig handover doc, dedicated sessions

2. The Three Change Questions

For every stakeholder group, answer three questions before writing any communication:

  1. What changes? The concrete difference in their Monday-morning routine — what they stop doing, start doing, or do differently. For a dispatcher: "You stop checking a shared inbox; leads arrive in your queue and you claim them there."
  2. Why now? The honest reason this change happens at this time — the business cost of the status quo (leads stagnating for two days) and the target (under four hours).
  3. What's in it for me (WIIFM)? The personal benefit framed for this audience, not for the sponsor. A dispatcher cares that leads arrive pre-assigned; a manager cares that the pipeline appears without asking someone to build a spreadsheet.

These three answers are the raw material of every training session, release note, and launch email in this phase. If you cannot answer one for a persona, the change is undefined — broadcasting an undefined change guarantees resistance.

3. Stakeholder and Persona Impact Assessment

Before building a training plan, build an impact assessment. This is the change-management version of the stakeholder map from Phase 2: power and interest tell you whom to manage closely; impact and readiness tell you what support each needs.

PersonaImpact (high/med/low)ReadinessSupport effort
Dispatcher (SME)High — new intake workflowHigh — championLight, peer-led
Sales repHigh — new record habitsMediumDemo + cheat sheet
Billing userMedium — fields movedMediumGuided walkthrough
Ops managerHigh — KPI dashboardLow — new reporting habitReport walkthrough

Two rules sharpen it: let the champion — the SME already excited — be the first wave of support, since a convincing peer beats any slide deck; and resist "support everyone equally" — spend effort where impact is high and readiness low, give low-impact groups self-service.

4. The WIIFM Conversation

People adopt what helps them and resist what looks like added work. WIIFM is not manipulation — it is translation: project goals into the user's daily reality. "≥80% of inbound leads auto-assigned" is a KPI; to a dispatcher it means "no more fishing leads out of a shared inbox."

Project goalUser-facing translation
Lead-to-dispatch under 4 hoursYou claim leads from your queue, not a mailbox
Auto-assignment without re-entryThe lead's company and route arrive already recorded
Duplicate suppressionYou do not call the same customer twice
Pipeline dashboard for managersYou see this week's freight at a glance, not Friday afternoons

Run WIIFM in the same sessions as training, headed by champions. The tone rule is constant: the change is a tool for the user's job, never a hoop. If the only honest WIIFM is "your boss wants it," say that and pair it with the fastest path through the new system.

5. Designing the Training Plan

A training plan maps persona to format to timing. It is a compromise between what is ideal (everyone gets days of hands-on practice) and what is real (people have jobs to do). The BrightLogistics training plan:

PersonaFormatTimingReinforce
Dispatchers2h live lab in a sandboxWeek of sign-offPeer office hours
Sales reps1.5h demo + recorded version1 week before go-liveCheat sheet, quick wins
Ops managers45-min report walkthroughLaunch dayWeekly pulse email
AdminsConfig handover doc + walkthroughAs builtOn-call support window

The plan names one owner per row, with reinforcement built in — training without it decays within days. Run the sessions in a sandbox so users practice on real objects without touching production, ideally right after UAT while scenarios are fresh.

6. Training Materials That Stick

Adults learn by doing, and they forget fast. Three material types carry most of the load, and all three are cheap to produce:

  • Cheat sheets — one side of paper, the 5–8 actions a persona does constantly. Rules: screenshots with arrows, no prose, no menu dives.
  • Recorded labs — the live training captured and searchable, so a rep remembers "how did I log that again?" at 9pm and finds the answer instead of emailing the admin.
  • Sandbox practice scenarios — three realistic exercises per persona: "Here are five web leads; route, claim, and log the follow-up." Recording a task in the system is worth ten slides about the system.

The test for any training material, like release notes: does it answer "what do I do differently on Monday?" If a user can follow the cheat sheet and complete a real task unaided, it works.

7. The Communication Plan

Communications run on a cadence, not a single launch email. Plan who hears what, through which channel, when. A simple comms plan for the rollout:

AudienceChannelCadenceMessage
All staffEmail + team standupWeekly, 4 weeks pre-launchWhat's happening and which date
DispatchersPeer office hoursTwice weekly after launchHow-to, live problem solving
ManagersDashboard + pulse reportWeeklyAdoption numbers and wins
ExecutivesSponsor dashboardWeeklyKPI progress only

Use channels users already read — BrightLogistics lives in email and the standup; do not invent a new tool to announce a new tool. Weekly repetition moots "we were never told." After launch the comms shift from announcement to reinforcement — wins, office hours, adoption trend.

8. Writing Release Notes

Release notes announce what changed, when it lands, and how users respond — in business language, not metadata speak. Nobody in ops cares that an object gained a field; they care that they no longer retype lead data.

md
Release 2.1 — what's new
NEW   Lead routing now assigns web leads in ~0 seconds (was up to 2 days)
CHANGED The "UAT readiness" board moved to the Dashboard tab
FIXED Case escalation no longer duplicates tasks
→ Training lab Feb 3 · Q&A after release

Four rules keep release notes honest and useful:

  1. List the top user-visible changes, not every field. If a user cannot see it, it is not a note — it is changelog noise.
  2. Group notes as New / Changed / Fixed. People scan by what they are looking for.
  3. Show a before-after for the biggest change. "~0s (was 2 days)" does more than a paragraph of praise.
  4. Publish in the channel users already read, and end with the training or Q&A invitation if the change needs one.

9. Measuring Adoption

Adoption is a number, not a feeling. Track genuine usage — logins, record creation, flow runs, report views — and compare it against two fixed points: a baseline (usage four weeks before go-live) and a target (the sponsor-agreed KPI, e.g. 70% of reps active within 60 days). The demo service that models the tracking lives in ChangeManagementService.cls:

apex
// ChangeManagementService tracks adoption on the Account.
// Adoption_Score__c = f(training completion, logins, UAT sign-off)
// Demo only - real adoption needs a Usage app or login metrics.

The metric set for BrightLogistics is deliberately small:

MetricBaseline (pre-launch)Target (day 60)
Active dispatchers0% (no system)≥80% active weekly
Leads created in CRM0All inbound, no re-entry
Flow runs (auto-assign)0≥80% of inbound leads
Manager dashboard views0Weekly per manager

Declining adoption is a signal to retrain, not rebuild. A mid-launch drop rarely means the config is wrong — it means people are drifting back to old habits; the fix is targeted training, refocused comms, or a simpler path, not reconstruction.

10. Adoption Dashboards and the Business_Analyst Permission Set

Adoption lives on a dashboard the sponsor opens weekly. The Business_Analyst permission set — used throughout this roadmap — grants access to the objects, reports, and dashboards behind it. Built with Phase 10 principles, it shows three or four components only:

  • Active users trend (line) — logins per persona against the 60-day target.
  • Flow run volume (bar) — auto-assignments by week, the core KPI.
  • Sign-off and training completion (gauge) — who finished the labs.
  • Open defects / known issues (list) — carried from UAT.

One discipline: measure per persona, not per org — "dashboard adoption" says nothing about dispatchers. Group by role so a drop in one persona is visible before it becomes a general decline.

11. Post-Launch Iteration: Retrain, Don't Rebuild

After go-live the change plan enters its most valuable stretch — the feedback loop. Set the cadence in advance: two weeks of office hours, weekly "ask the BA" slots, reviews at day 30 and 60 against targets. At each review:

  1. Are the targets being met per persona? (dashboard)
  2. What behaviors are users asking about? (office-hours log)
  3. What should change — the support, the message, or the system?

Rarely is the answer "the system": "where do I find X?" is training; no logins is motivation or comms; working around a step may point to config — confirm before changing anything. The UAT results and known-issues list from Phase 12 anchor these decisions.

12. Change Management Across the Delivery Life Cycle

Change management is not a phase that starts at launch; it is a thread through the whole roadmap. The stakeholder engagement in Phase 2 is the first communication plan; the as-is/to-be maps in Phase 3 are the first "what changes" statements; the UAT sign-off in Phase 12 is the first adoption event. Every artifact you produced earlier becomes change-manage material later.

The portfolio exercises celebrate this. Exercise 8.3 (Adoption Plan) builds a three-persona change plan with a KPI per persona; 9.1 (Portfolio Checklist) files your training plan and release notes as evidence; Phase 16's Use Case 3 is the full-length version. The habit to keep: every phase should name the people it changes.

Hands-On Exercises

1. Persona WIIFM Table

Write the three change questions for BrightLogistics staff.

Steps:

  1. List three personas: dispatcher, sales rep, ops manager.
  2. Answer "what changes," "why now," and "WIIFM" for each.
  3. Rewrite one project KPI in each persona's language.

Expected result: a table where nine cells prove the change is understood per audience.

What it proves: that any change is only ready to announce when you can answer WIIFM per persona.

2. Build the BrightLogistics Training Plan

Design the training plan for launch week.

Steps:

  1. Map each persona to a format, timing, trainer, and reinforcement step.
  2. Schedule sessions against the sign-off date and go-live date.
  3. Define the material set (cheat sheet, lab, recording).

Expected result: a one-page plan with no persona left without training and reinforcement.

What it proves: that training is a plan with owners and dates, matching Exercise 8.3.

3. Rewrite Release Notes

Take a raw changelog and turn it into user-facing notes.

Steps:

  1. List the top user-visible changes (max five) in business language.
  2. Group them as New / Changed / Fixed.
  3. Add a before-after line for the leading-change and the training invitation.

Expected result: notes a dispatcher can read in thirty seconds and act on Monday.

What it proves: the "business impact first" rule for all user-facing communication.

4. Adoption KPI Dashboard Spec

Spec the adoption dashboard for Greg.

Steps:

  1. Define three KPIs with baseline, target, and data source.
  2. Choose the chart type and drill-down for each.
  3. Name the refresh cadence and the persona tracked per metric.

Expected result: a dashboard spec where every KPI has numbers, dates, and an owner.

What it proves: that adoption is measured per persona against agreed numbers.

5. A 60-Day Support and Communication Calendar

Plan the post-launch reinforcement window.

Steps:

  1. List office hours, pulse emails, and weekly adoption review slots across 60 days.
  2. Mark the day-30 and day-60 decisions against the targets.
  3. Write the "what do we do if a target misses" action for each persona.

Expected result: a dated calendar with owners and fallback actions.

What it proves: that change management continues on a cadence after launch, with a retrain-don't-rebuild reflex.

Key Terms Glossary

TermDefinition
Change managementThe people-side plan: who is affected, what changes, how they are brought along
PersonaA role-based group sharing the same change and support needs
WIIFMWhat's in it for me — the personal benefit framed for a specific audience
Adoption readinessThe assessed impact and support effort per persona before launch
Training planThe persona → format → timing → reinforcement mapping
Cheat sheetA one-page reference of the constant actions a persona performs
Release notesUser-facing announcements written in business language, grouped New/Changed/Fixed
Communication planThe audience-channel-cadence schedule for a change
BaselinePre-go-live usage measured four weeks before launch
TargetThe sponsor-agreed adoption KPI, e.g. 70% active at day 60
Adoption metricA measured behavior: logins, record creation, flow runs, report views
Retrain, don't rebuildThe diagnosis reflex: declining adoption points to support, not configuration
Business_AnalystThe permission set granting access to the roadmap's objects, reports, and dashboards
Per-persona measurementTracking adoption by role rather than across the whole org

Certification Checkpoints

  • I can answer "what changes, why now, WIIFM" for every stakeholder persona.
  • I can write a training plan with format, timing, owner, and reinforcement per persona.
  • I can rewrite a raw changelog into business-language release notes.
  • I can build a communication plan with audience, channel, and cadence.
  • I can define adoption metrics against a baseline and a target.
  • I know why adoption must be measured per persona, not per org.
  • I apply "retrain, not rebuild" as the first response to declining usage.
  • I have completed Exercise 8.3 (Adoption Plan) in Phase 15.

Summary

You learned that the value of the rollout lives in changed behavior, not deployed code. You assessed adoption readiness by persona, answered the three change questions, designed training plans with reinforcement built in, and wrote release notes in language users actually read. You defined adoption as a measurable comparison between a pre-launch baseline and a sponsor-agreed target, surfaced it on a per-persona dashboard behind the Business_Analyst permission set, and committed to diagnosing any decline before rebuilding anything. The roadmap now hands you its final duty: turning everything you practiced into a passing pass at the Salesforce Certified Business Analyst exam.
